restart_api_pool.detail: Rolling restart of the payment-api workers dropped 5xx from 31% to ~12% and freed the pool, but the same v2.17.4 build is still running, so connections leak again.
restart_api_pool.lesson: Restarting payment-api pods produced only temporary improvement and then regression.
restart_api_pool.reusable_lesson: Restarting payment-api pods did not resolve Redis connection-pool exhaustion under this condition: the 5xx rate fell from 31% to about 12% for roughly 45 seconds and then returned to 31% because the leaking build was still deployed. Do not treat a pod restart as remediation for pool exhaustion; inspect the per-worker connection count and the deploy diff instead.
restart_api_pool.warning: Previous similar incident: restarting API pods produced only temporary improvement and regression.

rollback_recent_deploy.detail: Rolled payment-api back to v2.17.3. The leaking checkout path is gone, the per-worker pool drains back to ~63/100, and 5xx returns to the 0.4% baseline.
rollback_recent_deploy.lesson: Rolling back the leaking release fixed the incident; the leak was in the deployed version, not in the runtime.
rollback_recent_deploy.reusable_lesson: For payment-api Redis connection-pool exhaustion, rolling back the release that introduced the connection leak restores service (connections 100/100 -> ~63/100, 5xx 31% -> 0.4%).

increase_redis_pool_size.detail: Raised the per-worker Redis pool from 100 to 150 and lowered the acquisition timeout to 250ms. Buys headroom but the leak is still present, so saturation returns later; effective now, not durable.
increase_redis_pool_size.lesson: Increasing the pool size masked the exhaustion temporarily; capacity is finite and the leak remains, so this is a mitigation, not a fix.
increase_redis_pool_size.reusable_lesson: Increasing the payment-api Redis pool from 100 to 150 connections reduced 5xx to about 1-3% but the leak in v2.17.4 was still present; treat pool growth as a time-boxed mitigation, not a resolution.

scale_out_workers.detail: Adding 12 more workers made it worse: each new worker opened its own 100-connection pool, so Redis hit its client limit (10k) and 5xx climbed to 38%.
scale_out_workers.lesson: Scaling out amplified the pool problem because pool size is per worker.
scale_out_workers.reusable_lesson: Scaling payment-api out during a Redis pool exhaustion incident makes it worse: the connection budget is per worker, so extra workers consume more Redis connections.

flush_cache.detail: High-risk action: flushing the cart session cache would drop live carts. Blocked by the safety gate; if forced it would destroy in-flight checkout state.
flush_cache.lesson: Cache flush is destructive for cart sessions and was blocked; it does not fix a client-side pool leak.
flush_cache.reusable_lesson: Flushing the payment-api cart cache during an incident destroys in-flight checkout state and does not resolve a client-side connection leak.
